newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian stocks poised to move higher.
newsitem.headline: Croatian stocks poised to move higher.

text.p: Croatian stocks, basking in record highs and burgeoning turnover, look set to continue their winning ways as domestic investors join a foreign buying frenzy, analysts said on Wedensday.
"There is no reason for the current bull run not to last for a while," Ratko Bajakic, manager of recently-opened Investment Bank Austria, told Reuters.
The stampede began in the summer as foreign investors turned bullish after the resounding success of the flotation of Pliva and Zagrebacka on the London Stock Exchange.

The recent stock market rally, unimaginable earlier in the year when shares were sold in trickles at prices way below their issue price, was attributed by traders to a mixture of solid purchasing interest and pure speculation.
While market watchers said a few traded firms might suffer the effects of poor performance and unresolved ownership issues, they were optimistic a majority of stocks were poised for further gains.
But Igor Kos at brokers Taurus said stocks would likely face correction towards the end of October to consolidate the recent sharp gains as buying incentives ebb.
"Like everywhere else, there is bound to be some correction at some point," he said.
Publication of a list, due out later this month, of firms to be included in the mass voucher scheme was expected to have a longer-term dampening effect on prices.

Once the list appeared, speculative trading with shares of the firms on it would be halted amid worries that their value would go down as soon as beneficiaries of the scheme started to unload them indiscriminately, market participants said.
However, they said new interest among locals to invest in stocks, supported by large gains in blue chips and declining interest rates, would continue to wind up most prices.
A trend aided and abetted by the strong presence of foreigners, buying anything from cheap hotel issues to blue chips such as pharmaceutical firm Pliva and Zagrebacka Banka.
"Buy orders will drive the market for at least the next two weeks," Kos said. "People are buying everything, with or without a reason."
Both Pliva and Zagrebacka, which floated shares abroad earlier this year, are very attractive because their global depositary receipts (GDRs) can be traded at a profit in London.
Days with turnover spilling over 20 million kuna ($3.5 million) have long ceased being a rarity and trading volume has been booming almost daily.
However, traders warned the days were over when almost all prices were so low that any purchase was bound to pay off if the buyer sat on it for a while.
"Brokers are on a hunt for the next stock to be listed in London," said Velimir Zelimorski of brokerage Fima.

Rumours of talks between the most likely candidates -- confectioner Kras and food processor Podravka -- with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) added spice to market developments.
The EBRD had first granted a loan to Pliva and later bought an equity stake in it to spur its privatisation.
But both firms played down rumours that a deal with the bank was in sight and denied they were considering international flotation of their shares.
